what_this_file_is: The comparable cost layer. Every price in it was captured on 2026-08-18 and carries its currency and the exact URL it was read from. Nothing here is a new price: prices come from plans-vps-eu.json, plans-vps-us.json, plans-hyperscalers.json, plans-managed-wp.json, plans-paas.json and egress.json, with ten corrections from an adversarial re-fetch applied first and listed in corrections_applied. Everything else is arithmetic on those figures, and every derived number carries the formula that produced it. Where a figure could not be established without inventing one, the field is null and the reason is stated next to it. A null with a reason is the correct answer; a plausible figure would be a defect.
rules_observed: Every price carries its capture date (2026-08-18), its currency and the exact URL it was read from.
No number was invented. Behind a configurator, a login, a quote form or an unpinnable currency selector means null plus a reason.
The renewal price is treated as the primary field. Where a price is not promotional, is_promotional false is stated explicitly so the reader knows it was checked.

VAT treatment is stated per price, and null where the page does not say. The normalisation axis is ex-VAT throughout; the one inc-VAT seller, IONOS, is placed on that axis using its own published net figures, not a division performed here.
The billing period actually quoted is recorded, including where a monthly-looking rate needs a 12-month or 48-month prepayment.
Observations, not verdicts. No superlatives. No em-dashes.

fx.source: The currencyRates object in the inline JavaScript config of https://kinsta.com/pricing/, recorded verbatim in plans-managed-wp.json under Kinsta notes: 'a currencyRates object with EUR 0.871688'.
fx.why_this_one: It is the only USD-to-EUR rate published by any provider page in this dataset and captured on the same day as the prices, so it is traceable rather than invented. It is a display-conversion rate a vendor uses to render a price, not a rate anyone transacts at.
fx.status: INDICATIVE. Every EUR figure derived from a USD price in this file is an indication, not a quote. A reader who wants a different rate can re-run every formula, because every formula is printed alongside its result.

chf.reason: No CHF-to-EUR rate is published on any provider page in this dataset. Infomaniak is quoted in CHF and its own checkout is reported to switch to EUR for EU visitors behind a JavaScript configurator that was not operated. Converting would require an invented rate, so Infomaniak is excluded from every EUR normalisation and its native CHF metrics are given instead.

OVHcloud's public catalog for the Ireland storefront, https://eu.api.ovh.com/1.0/order/catalog/public/vps?ovhSubsidiary=IE, lists planCode vps-2027-model1 with three pricing modes: default (no commitment) EUR 4.49 per month, upfront6 EUR 4.26 per month on a 6-month commitment, and upfront12 EUR 3.81 per month on a 12-month commitment. Installation fees and upgrade fees are both 0. The advertised 3.81 is the upfront12 figure.
source_notes.renewal_note: Not promotional. In the same catalog the upfront12 pricing carries capacities: ["renew"] and commitment: 12, meaning EUR 3.81 per month is also the renewal rate on the same 12-month commitment. Separately, the instance price contains no storage at all: local storage is EUR 0.00014 per GiB-hour, about EUR 0.10 per GiB per month, so a 40 GB disk adds about EUR 4 per month on top. source_notes.price_note: The Standard Instances table prints only a "Price / Hour" column. For Micro that value is EUR 0.00729 per hour ex tax, served to the page from Exoscale's own endpoint https://portal.exoscale.com/api/pricing/opencompute under key running_micro. The monthly figure recorded, 5.25, is 720 x hourly, the multiplier Exoscale's own pricing script applies (scope.monthly_price = function(price){return 720*price} in https://www.exoscale.com/static/js/pricing.ng.js). It is a derivation from the provider's hourly price using the provider's own multiplier, not a number printed on the page. There is no commitment: the page says "no long-term commitments. Completely on-demand, you can start, stop and scale your usage with no penalties, paying only what you use."
source_notes.storage_note: Storage is not included in the instance price. The table footnote reads: "Local Storage is not included in the displayed Instances price, and has a cost of {volume price} EUR / GiB hour." That rate is EUR 0.00014 per GiB-hour, about EUR 0.10 per GiB per month. The row states a minimum local storage of 10 GB and a maximum of 200 GB, but since none of it is in the price, storage_gb and storage_type are null.
source_notes.transfer_note: Recorded as 1 because Exoscale states it in monthly terms itself: "Traffic is billed per GiB with a free tier of up to 1.42 GiB / hr granted per-Instance (equivalent to 1 TiB / mo per-Instance)." Note the unit is TiB, not TB. The allowance pools: "If an instance doesn't use its free tier, it is reported on other running instances of the same organization." Excess outbound is EUR 0.02 per GiB. Inbound, inter-zone and inter-instance traffic are all free.

Note 320 / 12 = 26.67, displayed as 27. transfer_tb 0.075 is the stated 75 GB per month. Add-ons priced on the same card: additional site +€19, Automated Plugin Updates +€3. method.cost_per_gb_ram: eur_per_gb_ram_month = price_eur_ex_vat_per_month / ram_gb. Computed on the RENEWAL price where one exists, because the renewal is what the buyer lives with; the same figure on the current price is carried in normalised_on_current_price on every plan.
method.vat_axis: Ex VAT. IONOS quotes inc-VAT at 19 percent and its net figures are taken from its own page payload (EUR 2.52 / 4.20 / 12.61 now, EUR 7.56 / 15.13 / 48.74 at renewal). Vultr, Azure and WP Engine state no VAT treatment at all; their figures are used as displayed and flagged.
method.currency_axis: EUR. USD converted once, at 0.871688, indicatively. CHF not converted at all.
method.what_a_null_means: A null in a normalised field always means the input spec is null or the price could not be placed on the EUR axis. It never means zero. Every such plan is listed in excluded_plans below with its reason.
method.a_warning_about_vcpu: The per-vCPU figures are published but are the weaker of the two metrics, because a vCPU is not a comparable unit across sellers. Google's own documentation records e2-small's 2 listed vCPUs as 0.5 guaranteed; Hetzner's CPX line is shared AMD and its CCX line is dedicated at roughly four times the price for the same count; Azure's B-series bank credits and throttle to a 20 or 30 percent baseline. Cost per GB of RAM has no equivalent ambiguity, which is why it leads the tables.

vps_cheapest_per_provider_eur_per_gb_ram.caveat: THE HEADLINE RATE REQUIRES A 12-MONTH PREPAYMENT. The page prints 'From EUR 19.96 ex. VAT/month'; 'From' is a commitment tier, not an introductory offer. The same catalog prices this plan at EUR 23.49 per month with no commitment and EUR 22.31 on 6 months. On the no-commitment rate the cost per GB of RAM is EUR 0.9787 rather than EUR 0.8317. Both are renewal rates: the upfront12 pricing carries capacities: ['renew'] and commitment: 12, so EUR 19.96 is also what you pay in year two on the same commitment.

NOT ORDERABLE AT CAPTURE. The row carried the label 'not available' (CSS class product-highlight-label-NotAvailable) on 2026-08-18. The page explains the Cost-Optimized range runs on older hardware and that 'this resource-saving use means that the number of available servers is limited'. The price endpoint still returns active=true for all three EU datacentres. These two rows carry Hetzner's lowest cost per GB of RAM and a reader cannot necessarily buy either of them. The cheapest Hetzner row with no availability label at capture is CPX32 at EUR 4.4988 per GB of RAM, which is 4.0 times CX33.

THE RANKED FIGURE IS THE RENEWAL, NOT THE HEADLINE. IONOS is the only seller here quoting inc-VAT and the only EU VPS seller with a genuine introductory rate. cost_with_1tb_egress.arithmetic: Kinsta is the one provider here where 1 TB has two legitimate answers, an order of magnitude apart, and the honest presentation is the range. Lower bound, everything served from the CDN: (1,000 - 125) x USD 0.05 = USD 43.75. Upper bound, everything served from the origin: (1,000 - 20) x USD 0.50 = USD 490.00.
cost_with_1tb_egress.caveat: Two acceleration clauses fire at this volume: server bandwidth over the plan by more than 250 GB is charged at the end of the first week following the overage, and an 'extreme overage' (as large as the plan cost, or USD 500, whichever is less) lets Kinsta act before the renewal date.

cost_with_1tb_egress.arithmetic: Netlify does not sell bandwidth in gigabytes, it sells credits. 1,000 GB x 20 credits per GB = 20,000 credits. Pro's base tier includes 3,000, so 17,000 must be bought. Add-on credits on Pro cost USD 10 per 1,500: 17,000 / 1,500 = 11.333 packs x USD 10 = USD 113.33. Per gigabyte that is 20 x (10 / 1500) = USD 0.1333.
cost_with_1tb_egress.caveat: The per-GB rate is DERIVED, not published: Netlify publishes the credit cost and the pack price separately and never prints a dollar-per-GB figure. On Personal, where packs are 500 credits for USD 5, the same traffic works out at about USD 0.40 per GB, three times the Pro rate.

cost_with_1tb_egress.arithmetic: No allowance at any tier, so the whole volume prices at the region-group rate: 1,000 GB x USD 0.02 = USD 20.00 for a machine in the North America or Europe group.
cost_with_1tb_egress.caveat: Region groups swing this six-fold on identical traffic: Asia Pacific, Oceania and South America are USD 0.04 per GB (USD 40.00), Africa and India USD 0.12 (USD 120.00). For scale, USD 20.00 of egress is roughly ten times the USD 1.94 per month it costs to keep the smallest machine running.

comparisons.title: VPS and cloud compute
comparisons.scope: One row per plan. EU, Swiss and US sellers in a single table with a jurisdiction chip, because a reader deciding between Hetzner and DigitalOcean should not have to open two pages. 28 rows.
comparisons.own_table_because: These are whole products: the headline figure buys CPU, RAM, disk, an IP address and, at most sellers, transfer. That is what makes them comparable with each other and not with the hyperscaler table.

columns.label: Provider and plan
columns.note: Jurisdiction shown as a two-letter chip after the name, from providers-merged.json.

columns.label: EUR / GB RAM
columns.unit: EUR per GB of RAM per month, ex VAT, at the renewal price
columns.note: The comparable number. USD sellers converted at one indicative rate, marked with a tilde.

columns.label: Year 2 / mo
columns.note: What you pay from month 13. For 24 of 28 rows this equals the headline. For the IONOS rows it does not.

columns.label: RAM / vCPU
columns.note: So the reader can see what the normalisation divided by.

columns.label: Transfer
columns.note: Null is shown as a dash with a footnote, never as zero.

default_sort.why: Sorting on headline price ranks the smallest box first, which tells a reader nothing: the cheapest row would be a plan with 2 GB of RAM. No two providers sell the same machine, so the only sort that answers 'who is cheap' is cost per unit of the thing you are buying. Ascending because the question readers arrive with is 'what is the cheapest way to get X'.

read_first.why: It is the one number nobody can compute at home, because it needs a currency conversion, a VAT adjustment and a spec division, and because RAM is the binding constraint on a small server far more often than vCPU is. The vCPU figure is published in the data but kept off the phone table: it separates dedicated from shared cores so poorly that Google's own docs describe e2-small's 2 listed vCPUs as 0.5 guaranteed.

comparisons.mobile: 5 columns. Row label wraps to two lines; the four data columns are numeric and short. No horizontal scroll at 390 px.
comparisons.excluded_rows: Infomaniak's three plans appear with a dash in the EUR column and a footnote, not a blank: they are quoted in CHF and no CHF-to-EUR rate exists in this dataset. Scaleway and Exoscale carry a storage footnote because their instance prices include no disk at all.

comparisons.title: Hyperscaler instances
comparisons.scope: AWS, Azure and Google small general-purpose instances in EU regions, plus each provider's free tier. 12 rows.
comparisons.own_table_because: A separate table is the only honest way to show these. A hyperscaler instance price buys compute and RAM and nothing else: no boot disk, no IPv4, no transfer, no backups. Putting a t4g.small in the same table as a Hetzner CX23 invites a comparison between a component and a product. The table therefore carries a standing banner, not a footnote.

columns.label: Instance / mo
columns.note: Marked ~ where converted from USD.

columns.label: + 1 TB egress
columns.note: The point of the table.

columns.label: Egress vs instance
columns.note: How many times the instance price the traffic costs.

columns.label: Also billed
columns.note: Disk, IPv4, load balancer, backups, support. Tapping expands the list.

default_sort.why: Sorting on the instance price alone reproduces exactly the error the table exists to correct. The all-in figure is the only sort that keeps the reader honest, and it reorders the table: of the two providers offering a like-for-like 2 vCPU / 2 GiB shape, Google's e2-small is the cheaper instance (EUR 11.73 against AWS t4g.small at EUR 12.22) and the more expensive line once 1 TB of traffic is added (EUR 109.15 against EUR 82.82), because europe-west1 on Premium Tier has no free egress row at all while AWS gives the account 100 GB.

read_first.why: It is the finding. On an AWS t4g.small at EUR 12.22 per month, 1 TB of egress adds EUR 70.60, which is 5.8 times the machine. Nobody shopping on the instance price would guess that, and no hyperscaler pricing page puts the two numbers on the same screen.

comparisons.mobile: 5 columns, all short. The 'Also billed' column is a count with a tap-to-expand, so it costs one character of width.

comparisons.title: What you pay in year two
comparisons.scope: Every plan in the dataset flagged promotional after correction. 12 rows.
comparisons.own_table_because: This is the site's reason to exist and it should not be a column buried in four other tables. It also has a shape the other tables do not: two totals and a multiple, with a null that is itself the story.

columns.label: Year 1 total
columns.note: Not 12 x the headline. It is months-at-promo plus months-at-renewal, and for Kinsta it is 11 months, not 12.

columns.label: Year 2 total
columns.note: Rendered as 'not published' in bold where the provider does not publish one. Never blank.

columns.label: Times more
columns.note: Year two divided by year one.

columns.label: Cliff at month
columns.note: 4 for IONOS, 13 for SiteGround, 49 for Hostinger's 48-month term, 2 for Kinsta's free month.

default_sort.why: The reader is here for the worst case. Descending puts the 5.35x at the top and the 1.0x rows at the bottom, which also makes the honest sellers visible by their position rather than by a badge.

read_first.why: Year one is the number every other comparison site prints. Year two is the number the buyer actually lives with, and in three of these twelve rows it does not exist at any published URL, which is a fact the column has to be able to say out loud.

comparisons.mobile: 5 columns. 'Cliff at month' is one or two digits.
comparisons.empty_state: If a category has no promotional plans, say so in a sentence rather than showing an empty table. US VPS, hyperscaler on-demand and PaaS all have zero rows here, and that is a finding worth printing.

comparisons.title: Managed WordPress and shared hosting
comparisons.scope: WP Engine, Kinsta, SiteGround, Hostinger. 12 rows.
comparisons.own_table_because: Not one plan in this category publishes a vCPU or a RAM figure, so the VPS table's normalisation cannot run on it. The category sells sites, storage, visits and bandwidth instead, and needs its own denominator.

columns.label: EUR / 1k visits
columns.unit: EUR per 1,000 monthly visits at the renewal price
columns.note: Dash plus footnote where the plan states no visit limit. A dash is not a zero and it is not 'unlimited'.

columns.label: Year 2 / mo
columns.note: 'Not published' for WP Engine.

columns.label: Over the cap
columns.note: The marginal price, which at WP Engine is roughly double its own average and at Kinsta is about half.

default_sort.why: Visits are what these plans meter and what a buyer can actually forecast. Rows with no stated limit sort last, not first, so an unpublished ceiling never wins a ranking by being blank.

read_first.why: It reverses the headline order. On the headline monthly, SiteGround StartUp at EUR 2.99 looks like a tenth of Kinsta's entry tier; per 1,000 visits SiteGround cannot be placed on the axis at all because it publishes no cap, and Kinsta's entry tier at about EUR 0.87 per 1,000 visits is cheaper than WP Engine's Startup at EUR 1.08.

comparisons.mobile: 5 columns; the overage column shows one figure and a unit chip.

comparisons.title: PaaS and edge platforms
comparisons.scope: Vercel, Netlify, Fly.io, Render, Railway. 22 rows including free tiers and quote-led tiers.
comparisons.own_table_because: The bill here is a small fixed fee plus metered usage, so the plan price is close to meaningless on its own: Render's Hobby workspace is USD 0 and buys no compute at all. The comparable numbers are the always-on floor and the unit rates, which no other category needs.

columns.label: Plan fee / mo
columns.note: Marked 'floor' where the fee is a spend minimum that includes usage credit rather than an addition, which is true of Railway Hobby and Pro.

columns.label: Cheapest always-on
columns.note: What it costs to keep one small thing running 24/7, on top of the fee.

columns.label: Egress / GB
columns.note: Derived and marked as such for Netlify, which prices bandwidth in credits and never publishes a dollar-per-GB figure.

default_sort.why: The plan fee is the number these vendors market and the least informative column on the row. Sorting on the always-on floor answers the question people actually arrive with, which is what the smallest real deployment costs.

read_first.why: It is where the category separates by a factor of seven and a half on identical traffic: Fly.io USD 20, Railway USD 50, Netlify USD 113.33, Render USD 149.25 on Hobby, Vercel USD 0 on Pro with zero headroom. The plan fees, at USD 0 to USD 25, are all within one restaurant meal of each other.

comparisons.mobile: 5 columns. Free and quote-led rows collapse into a sub-group by default so the table opens at 11 priced rows.

comparisons.title: What 1 TB of traffic costs
comparisons.scope: One row per provider, 21 rows, cutting across all categories. The only cross-category table.
comparisons.own_table_because: Egress is the single largest hidden variable in the dataset and it is invisible inside the per-category tables, because it is priced on a different page from the plan at almost every provider. It also produces the widest spread of any metric here: EUR 0.00 to USD 490.

columns.label: 1 TB costs
columns.note: Kinsta shows a range, not a point, because the answer depends on origin versus CDN.

columns.label: Headroom
columns.note: 0 percent on Vultr, Akamai and Vercel Pro, where the scenario lands exactly on the line.

default_sort.why: Almost half the rows are zero, so an ascending sort opens on a wall of zeroes and buries the finding. Descending opens on Kinsta's upper bound and Google's USD 111.76 and works down to the free half, which is the shape of the story.

read_first.why: A zero cost with zero headroom is a different product from a zero cost with 95 percent headroom, and the cost column cannot tell them apart. Hetzner uses 4.9 percent of its allowance on this scenario; Vultr, Akamai and Vercel Pro use exactly 100 percent, so one extra gigabyte starts a bill.

comparisons.mobile: 5 columns, all numeric or short chips.

comparisons.title: Who you are actually contracting with
comparisons.scope: One row per provider, 21 rows. This is the whole of the legal material on the redesigned site, on one page.
comparisons.own_table_because: The brief reduces legal to a single page, and a single page needs a single table. Collapsing it to one row per provider also stops legal facts leaking back into the cost tables as extra columns, which is what made the old structure unreadable on a phone.

columns.label: Contracts from
columns.note: The incorporation country of the entity that takes your money, not the location of the servers.

columns.label: Owned by
columns.note: Null where no parent could be established from a primary source, which is true of 9 of the 21 and is shown as 'not established' rather than 'independent'.

columns.label: US law reach
columns.note: 13 of 21 are direct.

columns.label: EU regions
columns.note: Zero for Infomaniak, which is Swiss only, and Switzerland is not in the EU.

default_sort.direction: none identified first, then by contracting country
default_sort.why: This is the one table where the reader usually arrives with a filter rather than a ranking: they want to see the EU-contracting options together. Sorting by exposure groups them without ranking anything, and no numeric sort would be meaningful across a column of country codes.

read_first.why: It is the fact most often confused with server location. Kinsta contracts from the US and runs in six EU regions; Infomaniak contracts from Switzerland and runs in none, because Switzerland is not the EU. Server location is the field readers look at and the contracting entity is the field that decides which court hears a dispute.

comparisons.mobile: 5 columns; 'Owned by' truncates to the parent name with tap-to-expand for the shareholding detail.

comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.claim: A cross-provider ranking that includes Infomaniak in EUR
comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.why: Infomaniak's public pages render CHF server-side in every locale tested and its checkout, which reportedly resolves to EUR ex VAT for an EU visitor, is a JavaScript configurator that was not operated. No CHF-to-EUR rate is published anywhere in this dataset. Its three plans carry native CHF metrics and a dash on the EUR axis.

comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.claim: Any year-two figure for WP Engine
comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.why: WP Engine publishes no renewal price at any URL. The static HTML, the configurator's JSON payload and the live configurator were all checked, and the signup flow redirects unauthenticated visitors back to the plans page. The only statement on the page is 'Product renewal pricing subject to change.' Three plans, EUR 320 charged up front on the smallest, and no published year two.

comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.claim: A price-per-GB-of-RAM figure for managed WordPress or shared hosting
comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.why: Not one of the twelve plans in that category publishes a vCPU or RAM figure. That is how the category is sold, not a gap in the capture. Cost per 1,000 monthly visits is the substitute, and even that runs on only six of the twelve rows because SiteGround and Hostinger publish no visit cap either.

comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.claim: Hyperscaler instance prices set beside VPS prices as like-for-like
comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.why: The hyperscaler figure buys compute and RAM and excludes the boot disk, outbound transfer, a public IPv4 address, load balancing, backups and support. Four of those are bundled into the headline figure at every VPS seller in this dataset. The tables can sit next to each other; the numbers cannot sit in one sorted column without a banner.

Microsoft prices Azure in USD and converts to EUR once a month at a London closing spot rate, and says so on the page and in its API documentation: 'Other non-USD prices returned by the API are for your reference to help you estimate budget expenses.' This dataset also carries two different EUR monthlies for the same USD 0.048 per hour, EUR 30.7868 from the page and EUR 30.733 from the API, which is why the B2s row is excluded from the ranking.

comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.claim: Included transfer for Hetzner read off a Hetzner plan page
comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.why: The two source files disagree. plans-vps-eu.json records transfer_tb null for all four plans and states that no TB figure appears on any of the five Hetzner pages it checked. egress.json records 20,480 GB from https://docs.hetzner.com/robot/general/traffic/, which the plans file did not check. The 1 TB scenario here uses the egress file's source and the disagreement is printed on every Hetzner row rather than resolved.

comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.claim: A single 1 TB egress figure for Kinsta
comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.why: It has two legitimate answers an order of magnitude apart depending on whether the bytes leave from the CDN at USD 0.05 per GB or the origin at USD 0.50 per GB: USD 43.75 against USD 490.00. Anything between them would be a guess about a reader's cache hit rate. The range is published and no point estimate is.

comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.claim: Cost per vCPU as a cross-seller ranking
comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.why: The figures are computed and published, but a vCPU is not one unit. Google documents e2-small's 2 listed vCPUs as 0.5 guaranteed; Hetzner's CCX dedicated line costs about four times its CPX shared line at the same vCPU count; Azure B-series throttle to a 20 or 30 percent baseline once credits are spent. The column exists in the data and is deliberately kept off the phone table.

comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.claim: Regional prices at Vultr, or per-configuration prices at Infomaniak VPS Cloud, or WP Engine's Core and Enterprise tiers
comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.why: All sit behind a logged-in control panel, a JavaScript configurator or a quote form. Vultr's own FAQ says location pricing 'is always available in the Control Panel', which is a login. Infomaniak VPS Cloud publishes only a 'From CHF 38.41' header against a stated minimum configuration. Recorded null.

comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.claim: Any statement that a provider is cheapest overall
comparisons_the_data_cannot_support.why: Cheapest per GB of RAM, cheapest with 1 TB of traffic and cheapest in year two are three different orderings in this dataset, and adding backups or support reorders them again. The tables give the reader the axis; the site does not pick one for them.
